prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Slugs are portrayed as strange, vulnerable creatures whose minimal features and nearly imperceptible movement make them seem like living soil.
- Their silvery trails provide the main evidence of their passage, while their deaths occur silently through crushing, salt, urine, or sharp objects.
- The speaker feels frustrated by the slugs’ passivity and urges them to resist rather than simply endure harm.
- The slugs are compared to smaller schoolboys who stood helplessly crying and sniffling while anticipating violence.
- The poem links helplessness with cruelty, showing how the victims’ visible fear and inability to fight back encouraged the bullies to continue attacking them.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Who, Small, Turn

outputs.L1:
Who could have dreamed them up? At least snails  
have shells, but all these have is—nothing.  
Small black antennae, like fat pins, wave  
as if they could take in enough to get them through.  
Turn them over: they’re the soles of new shoes,  
pale and unmarked as babies. They flow,  
the soil itself learning how to move and, moving,  
almost staying still, their silver monorail  
the only evidence of where they’ve been.

And they die quietly, or at least—thankfully—  
beyond the range of the human ear: between two stones,  
under heels, shriveling in salt or piss, at the tips  
of sharp sticks. Fight back, I hear myself say.  
Do something. Don’t just take it. But they die  
as they lived, exuding slime, like  
the smaller boys, who would simply  
stand there, miserable in short pants,  
school socks down around their ankles,  
school ties unknotted and askew, while slow cauls  
of snot flowed from their noses. From time to time,  
they would lick or sniff them partway back up  
until they flowed again, coating  
the upper lip, falling into the mouth, mingling  
with tears before anything had even been done—  
the fear itself enough—so that, even if we wanted to,  
we couldn’t let them off. Sometimes it was  
the knee “where you daren’t show your mother”;  
other times, the kick in the shins, the stick over  
the head, the punch in the mouth, while they  
just stood there or doubled over, gasping  
for breath—and we did it again.
outputs.L2:
Who might have imagined creatures like these? Snails, after all, carry their own armor; these beings possess no protection whatsoever. Their stubby dark feelers, thick as pinheads, sway about as though sensing the world might be enough to sustain them. Flip one onto its back and its underside resembles an unworn shoe sole—light-colored, spotless, infant-soft. They glide as if earth had discovered motion, advancing so slowly they seem nearly motionless. Only the gleaming track behind them reveals their passage.

Their deaths make no audible sound—or none that people can hear, fortunately. They perish crushed between rocks or beneath shoes, dried up by salt or urine, or pierced on sharpened twigs. I find myself urging them to resist, to react, not simply endure. Yet they meet death as they passed through life: releasing mucus.

They remind me of the younger, smaller schoolboys. Those children would remain rooted in place, wretched in their shorts, socks sagging around their ankles and ties hanging loose and crooked. Thick, membrane-like streams ran slowly from their nostrils. Occasionally they licked them away or drew them halfway back with a sniff, but the mucus always descended again, spreading over the top lip and entering the mouth, joining their tears before we had even begun. Their terror alone rendered them helpless, and because of that, even when we might have wished to spare them, we felt unable to do so.

Sometimes we kneed them in the place they would never dare mention to their mothers. At other times we struck their shins with our feet, brought a stick down on their heads, or hit them in the mouth. They merely remained upright—or folded inward, struggling to breathe—and then we attacked once more.
outputs.L3:
Slugs are portrayed as strange and intensely vulnerable creatures. Their bodies have few distinguishable features, and their movement is so slow that it is almost impossible to detect. As a result, they seem less like animals than pieces of living soil, closely connected to the ground across which they crawl. The clearest evidence of their movement is the silvery trail they leave behind. In contrast, their deaths often occur without warning or protest: they are crushed underfoot, killed with salt or urine, or pierced by sharp objects.

The speaker responds to this vulnerability with frustration as well as sympathy. Rather than accepting the slugs’ passive endurance, the speaker urges them to resist and defend themselves. Their helplessness reminds the speaker of smaller schoolboys who, when threatened with violence, could do little more than cry and sniffle as they waited to be attacked. This comparison broadens the poem’s focus from cruelty toward animals to bullying among humans.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that helplessness can provoke further cruelty. The victims’ visible fear and inability to fight back do not inspire mercy in the bullies; instead, they encourage the attacks to continue. Through the parallel between the slugs and the schoolboys, the poem exposes the disturbing way in which vulnerability can become an invitation to violence for those who enjoy exercising power over weaker beings.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents slugs as small, silent, and almost completely defenseless creatures. Their soft bodies and slow movements make them especially vulnerable, while their inability to cry out means that their suffering can easily be ignored. Through vivid physical imagery, the poet draws attention to their fragility and encourages the reader to see them not as disgusting pests but as living beings exposed to casual cruelty.

The slugs are compared at length to schoolboys who are bullied because they appear weak, frightened, or different. Like the slugs, these boys cannot protect themselves or respond effectively to violence. Their fear does not inspire sympathy in their tormentors; instead, it marks them as easy targets. The comparison transforms the treatment of the slugs into a broader reflection on human behavior, showing how cruelty often depends on an imbalance of power.

Most disturbingly, the poem suggests that passivity can provoke further aggression. Because the victims do not fight back, the bullies feel free to continue and even intensify their attacks. Helplessness, which should awaken compassion, becomes an invitation to violence. The attackers interpret silence as weakness and vulnerability as permission, revealing the twisted logic through which bullying justifies itself.

By linking animal suffering with the persecution of vulnerable children, the poem exposes brutality as a deeply human problem. It asks readers to consider why weakness so often attracts contempt rather than care and why fear can encourage cruelty instead of mercy. Ultimately, the slugs’ silent suffering becomes a powerful symbol of all defenseless victims, challenging us to recognize vulnerability and respond with empathy rather than violence.
outputs.L5:
**A Small Turn**

“Who are you?” the old man asked.

The child smiled and pointed to the narrow road ahead. “Someone taking a small turn.”

The old man looked at the wide highway behind them, crowded with noise and hurry. Then he followed the child down the quiet path.

Sometimes, a small turn is all it takes to discover who we are.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about slugs that gradually becomes a disturbing childhood memory of bullying vulnerable schoolboys.
counterfactuals.output:
After rain, the slugs came out  
like wet commas,  
small pauses glistening  
between the garden wall  
and the drain.

We watched their blind heads  
test the morning,  
each soft body carrying  
its one silver sentence  
across the blacktop.

Someone fetched salt.

At first, nobody spoke.  
The bell had not rung.  
Our shoes were new enough  
to reflect the sky.

We made a circle.

Years later, I remember  
how quickly a circle becomes  
a wall—  
how laughter closes gaps,  
how a boy with bitten sleeves  
can stand in the middle  
holding his satchel to his chest  
as if it were a door.

There was always one  
who walked too carefully,  
one whose lunch smelled different,  
one who flinched before being touched.

We called them names  
until their own names  
seemed weak and distant,  
something their mothers used  
in kitchens full of steam.

We flicked their ears.  
We tipped their books  
into puddles.  
We asked if they were going to cry  
in the bright, interested voices  
of children examining an insect.

And they tried not to.

That was the worst of it:  
the brave little tightening  
of the mouth,  
the eyes fixed somewhere beyond us,  
as though a narrow path  
still existed  
through our ring of polished shoes.

The teacher’s window shone above.  
No face appeared.

On the pavement,  
the slugs curled inward  
under their sudden weather.

One boy knelt to gather  
his soaked papers.  
His hands left faint marks  
on the ground—

not silver,  
not beautiful,

but I followed them home  
all the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark literary poem comparing the helplessness of slugs being killed to children passively enduring violence in a schoolyard.
counterfactuals.output:
**After Rain**

The slugs came out when the bell had rung,  
small commas shining on the concrete,  
soft-bodied, carrying no defense  
but silence and a borrowed gleam.

Shoes found them.

No anger—only the idle law  
of weight descending, laughter passing,  
the playground’s bright machinery  
turning tenderness to stain.

By the fence, the children watched,  
or learned the art of looking down.  
Some stood still while harsher hands  
made lessons of their shoulders.

They did not cry. The noon went on.  
A whistle split the air, too late.  
Clouds dragged their bruises over the roofs;  
teachers gathered papers from the wind.

Afterward, rain touched every mark—  
the silver trails, the scuffed blacktop,  
the places where the smallest lives  
had waited for the world to stop.

But mercy, like a distant bell,  
was heard and never came.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a visceral, first-person poem about cruelty, using snail-like slime, school uniforms, tears, and memories of tormenting smaller boys.
counterfactuals.output:
I wore my school uniform like a borrowed threat—  
tie knotted hard, shoes black as shut eyes,  
my name stitched neat above the heart  
I was trying not to have.

Behind the gym, the walls sweated rain.  
A snail dragged its silver wound across the bricks,  
slow, soft, leaving proof it had been there.  
I crushed it with one heel  
because I knew the smaller boys were watching.

I knew their shoulders: folded paper.  
I knew how fear makes a face go young.  
I called them names until each word stuck,  
snail-slime on their collars,  
gleaming, impossible to wipe away.

One boy cried without sound.  
His tears hung under his lashes  
like glass about to break.  
I laughed first. The others followed.  
That was the trick of cruelty—  
strike the match, then blame the fire.

Years later, I still wake tasting the corridor:  
chalk dust, wet wool, metal radiators,  
the sour shine of my own spit.  
Memory crawls back over me,  
cold-bellied, patient,  
leaving its trail across my skin.

I see my fist around a smaller wrist.  
I feel how little it was.  
That is what sickens me most—  
not that I was strong,  
but that I needed him weaker  
to feel my own body fill the uniform.

Now every tear I forced from them  
has found its way into my mouth.  
Salt. Salt.  
I cannot swallow enough forgiveness.

In dreams, the snail is whole again.  
It climbs my polished shoe,  
across the school crest, toward my throat.  
I do not crush it.

I stand there, finally small,  
while all the boys I tormented  
walk past without looking,  
and the silver trail closes over my voice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a contemporary poem that begins by closely observing slugs—their antennae, pale undersides, and silver trails—before shifting into a confession about childhood bullying.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk, the slugs come out  
wearing the rain like a second skin.

Their antennae test the air—  
two black questions lifted  
above the grass.

Underneath, they are pale,  
soft-footed, almost luminous,  
their bodies making one long decision  
against the concrete.

By morning, silver trails  
cross the garden path:  
small signatures,  
evidence of having gone on.

I used to pour salt on them.

There.  
That is not the worst thing  
I did as a child.

The worst was a boy named Michael  
whose coat smelled of wet wool,  
whose lunch came wrapped in foil  
and unfamiliar bread.

We learned how easily a person  
could be made into weather:  
a cold front in the hallway,  
a storm everyone saw coming  
and no one stopped.

I called him names  
because the others did,  
because laughter opened its bright door  
and I wanted in.

Years later, I still see him  
drawing his arms close,  
as if trying to become smaller  
than the body we had chosen for him.

Sometimes after rain  
I find a slug on the steps  
and lift it with a leaf,  
carry it past the gravel.

It leaves its silver sentence  
across my hand—

not forgiveness,  
not even a word,

only the shining fact  
that tenderness arrives late  
and must arrive anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
